items.followUp: Explain how an enzyme's active site changes when a substrate binds.

rubric.why: The induced-fit model describes an active site that is flexible before the substrate binds.
rubric.description: States that the active site is flexible and not a rigid, exact fit before binding.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the active site as flexible or not an exact fit before binding.

rubric.why: Substrate binding changes the active site's shape, allowing binding and formation of the enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.description: Explains that the substrate induces a shape change that allows it to fit the active site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking substrate binding with a change in the active site's shape and resulting fit or complex formation.

modelAnswer: According to the induced-fit model, an enzyme's active site is flexible and is not an exact fit for the substrate before binding.
When the substrate binds, it induces a change in the shape of the active site so that the substrate fits and an enzyme-substrate complex forms.

rubric.why: Saturated fatty acids have no carbon-carbon double bonds.
rubric.description: States that the carbon chain has only single bonds between carbon atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the absence of carbon-carbon double bonds.

rubric.why: The absence of carbon-carbon double bonds allows the chain to carry the maximum possible number of hydrogen atoms.
rubric.description: States that the fatty acid carries the maximum possible number of hydrogen atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining saturation in terms of hydrogen.

modelAnswer: Saturated fatty acids have carbon chains in which all carbon-carbon bonds are single bonds.
They carry the maximum possible number of hydrogen atoms.

items.followUp: State two roles of red blood cells.

rubric.why: Platelets help form a blood clot at an injury.
rubric.description: States that platelets help blood to clot.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying blood clotting or coagulation as the function of platelets.

rubric.why: Clotting seals the injured area and helps prevent blood loss.
rubric.description: States the protective result of clotting.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking clotting with stopping bleeding or preventing blood loss.

modelAnswer: Platelets help the blood to clot at the site of an injury.
The clot seals the damaged blood vessel and helps prevent blood loss.

items.followUp: Define tissue level and give an example of an organ system.

rubric.why: An organ is formed from different tissues that work together to perform a specific function.
rubric.description: Defines the organ level of organization.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that different tissues combine to form an organ and perform a function.

rubric.why: An organ system consists of a group of organs working together.
rubric.description: Defines the organ-system level of organization.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying an organ system as a group of organs that work together.

rubric.why: The organs in a system cooperate to carry out a major body function.
rubric.description: Explains the role of organs working together in an organ system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the organs cooperate to carry out a body function.

rubric.why: A suitable example shows how the organ-system level is organized.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of an organ system and relevant organs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a correct organ system and relevant organs.

modelAnswer: Organ level: Different tissues combine and work together to perform a specific function, forming an organ.
Organ-system level: A group of organs that work together to perform a major function of the body forms an organ system.
For example, the digestive system includes organs such as the stomach and intestines.
These organs work together to digest food and absorb nutrients.

items.followUp: Draw and label a plant cell, and state two functions of its nucleus.

rubric.why: The nucleus controls and coordinates the activities of the cell.
rubric.description: States the controlling role of the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying control or coordination of cell activities.

rubric.why: The nucleus contains hereditary material that carries genetic information.
rubric.description: States that the nucleus contains genetic or hereditary material.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying DNA, genes, chromosomes, or hereditary information in the nucleus.

rubric.why: The nucleus is enclosed by a double nuclear membrane with pores.
rubric.description: Describes the nuclear envelope and its pores.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the double membrane or envelope and pores.

rubric.why: Nucleoplasm, nucleolus, and chromatin or chromosomes are important nuclear components.
rubric.description: Names internal components of the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly naming the nucleoplasm, nucleolus, and chromatin or chromosomes.

rubric.why: A labelled diagram should show the nuclear boundary and internal structures.
rubric.description: Provides a clear labelled nucleus diagram showing the boundary and internal components.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a diagram with a double boundary and correctly labelled pores and internal components.

modelAnswer: The nucleus is a prominent cell organelle that controls and coordinates the activities of the cell.
It contains hereditary material (DNA), which carries information for the cell's characteristics and activities.
The nucleus is enclosed by a double nuclear membrane, also called the nuclear envelope, which has pores.
The interior contains nucleoplasm, a nucleolus, and chromatin; chromatin condenses to form chromosomes during cell division.

Diagram construction: Draw a roughly circular nucleus with a double outline. Add small gaps or dots on the outline for nuclear pores. Inside, show and label nucleoplasm, a nucleolus, and threads of chromatin. Label the double outline nuclear envelope.
